title: Patient Education Video Translation for Healthcare
summary: Compare subtitles, voiceover, and AI dubbing for patient education video translation, with checks for accuracy, access, cost, and follow-up.
body_markdown:
###


Choose the format that matches the patient's reading needs, viewing setting, and clinical risk. Subtitles work well for silent viewing but require reading; voiceover reduces reading demand; AI dubbing can sound natural but needs checks on drug names, doses, and negations before release. Test the finished video with teach-back before distribution, no matter which method you choose.


###


Review the written transcript first because any error there can carry through to the translated audio. Check every drug name, number, unit of measure, and negative word such as “not” or “don't” against the approved source script. Then confirm that pacing matches on-screen actions for medication and preparation instructions.


###


Translated subtitles convey dialogue in another language. Accessible captions also identify speakers and relevant sounds, such as alarms or notifications. Keeping captions with voiceover or AI dubbing helps patients who cannot play audio, use bedside devices, or prefer to read along.


###


Voiceover usually reduces barriers when patients have lower literacy in their preferred language because it removes the reading burden. Subtitles still work well for silent viewing contexts, such as waiting rooms or bedside tablets without headphones. Offering voiceover and captions together gives patients more ways to understand the same instruction.


###


Opalite Health is one of the broadest AI-native medical interpretation options for healthcare teams that need live follow-up after translated videos. It supports more than 150 languages and dialects through real-time AI medical interpretation, helping providers review instructions, ask teach-back questions, and create provider-reviewed draft notes through multilingual AI scribing.
